source_refs.note: Chapter 17 exercise (PDF 115-117, printed 111-113), solved: 10 MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to 7 short, 7 constructed and 6 comprehensive questions, and 6 numericals worked step by step.

blocks.prompt: 17.1 Name of device that is used as a part of charging circuit for mobile phones is:
blocks.explanation: Mobile phone chargers typically use a full-wave bridge rectifier, which converts the AC from the wall outlet into the DC needed to charge the phone's battery (17.14).

blocks.prompt: 17.2 A 10 μF capacitor is plugged into a 110 Vᵣₘₛ, 60 Hz voltage source, with an ammeter in series. The value of Iᵣₘₛ that passes through the capacitor is:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (d) is printed "0.0415 Ma". The symbol for milliampere is mA (Ma would read as mega-ampere); in any case 0.0415 mA is not the answer.

blocks.prompt: 17.3 In an RC-circuit a 10 kΩ resistance is connected in series to a capacitor of 0.05μF. The applied voltage for charging is 36 V, the RC-time constant to charge capacitor is:
blocks.explanation: Time constant τ = RC = (10 × 10³ Ω)(0.05 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 5 × 10⁻⁴ s = 0.5 ms. It does not depend on the 36 V. No option is exactly 0.5 ms; (c) 0.549 ms is the nearest and is the intended answer (see the box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: None of the printed options equals the RC-time constant: τ = RC = 0.5 ms. Option (c) 0.549 ms = RC × ln 3, which is the time the capacitor takes to charge to 2/3 of 36 V (24 V), not the time constant. (c) is keyed as the intended answer.

blocks.prompt: 17.4 In a purely inductive or capacitive circuit, the average power consumed is:
blocks.explanation: Voltage and current differ in phase by 90°, so P = VI cos 90° = 0. The energy stored in the magnetic (or electric) field in one quarter-cycle is returned to the source in the next (17.6, 17.8).

blocks.prompt: 17.5 Through which of the AC-circuit elements both emf and current are in phase?
blocks.explanation: In a resistor V = Vₒ sin ωt and I = Iₒ sin ωt: both reach their maximum and minimum values at the same time (17.5). In an inductor the current lags by 90°; in a capacitor it leads by 90°.

blocks.prompt: 17.6 An inductor with a reactance of 120 Ω, a capacitor with a reactance of 150 Ω and a 24 Ω resistance are connected in series across a 220 V source. When the circuit is at resonance, then voltage across the inductor is:
blocks.explanation:
At resonance X_L and X_C cancel, so Z = R = 24 Ω.
I = V/R = 220 V/24 Ω = 9.17 A
V_L = I X_L = 9.17 A × 120 Ω = 1100 V = 1.1 kV.
The voltage across the inductor is five times the source voltage (voltage amplification, 17.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: At resonance X_L = X_C, but the question gives 120 Ω and 150 Ω. The intended working takes Z = R at resonance and X_L = 120 Ω, giving 1.1 kV (b). (With the two reactances as given, the circuit is not at resonance: Z = √(24² + 30²) = 38.4 Ω and V_L = 687 V, which is not an option.) Option (b) prints the unit as "KV"; the symbol is kV.

blocks.prompt: 17.7 If magnetic field is doubled in an inductor, then, magnetic energy density becomes:
blocks.explanation: Energy density = B²/2μₒ (Eq. 17.38), so it is proportional to B². Doubling B makes it (2)² = 4 times.

blocks.prompt: 17.8 RC-time constant is measured in:
blocks.explanation: RC has the unit ohm × farad = (V/A)(C/V) = C/A = C/(C s⁻¹) = second.

blocks.prompt: 17.9 Resonance frequency of RLC-series circuit is fᵣ.If the capacitance is made 4 time the initial value, then the resonance frequency becomes:
blocks.explanation: fᵣ = 1/(2π√LC), so fᵣ ∝ 1/√C. With 4C: fᵣ' = fᵣ/√4 = fᵣ/2, i.e. half.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "4 time"; it means 4 times the initial value.

blocks.prompt: 17.10 The magnitude of mutual inductance M between two coils when current changes at 20 A s⁻¹ in one coil induces an emf of 50 mV in the other is:
17.1 What impacts does resistance have on capacitance?
blocks.explanation:
Resistance does not change the capacitance itself (C depends on the plate area, the separation and the dielectric).
It changes how the capacitor behaves in a circuit: a larger R charges and discharges the capacitor more slowly (time constant τ = RC), and in AC it adds to the impedance Z = √(R² + X_C²) and reduces the phase lead, θ = tan⁻¹(1/ωCR).

blocks.prompt: 17.2 What happens when an AC line touches a DC line?
blocks.explanation:
The two supplies are short-circuited together: the AC voltage is superimposed on the DC line, so it carries a fluctuating (DC + AC) voltage.
Large currents flow between the sources, causing sparking, overheating, blown fuses or tripped breakers, and damage to DC equipment (batteries, rectifiers, electronics); there is also a danger of electric shock. (beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: 17.3 What is the difference between peak to peak and amplitude in case of sine wave?
blocks.explanation: Amplitude is measured from zero to one peak; the peak-to-peak value is measured from the positive peak to the negative peak, so Vₚ₋ₚ = 2Vₒ.

rows: Highest value of the wave measured from zero (the zero line)
Total distance from the positive peak to the negative peak
Example: Vₒ = 311 V for 220 V mains

blocks.prompt: 17.4 Why are RC circuits used in timing circuits?
blocks.explanation:
A capacitor charges and discharges through a resistor at a fixed, predictable rate set by the time constant τ = RC.
By choosing R and C, any required time delay can be obtained, so RC circuits are used in timers, delay circuits, blinking lights and oscillators. (beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: 17.5 Why are choke coils preferred over resistors for limiting current in AC circuits?
blocks.explanation:
A choke has a large inductive reactance X_L = 2πfL but negligible resistance, so its power factor cos θ ≈ 0 (θ ≈ 90°).
It limits the current with practically no power lost as heat, whereas a resistor limits current by wasting energy as I²R heat.

blocks.prompt: 17.6 Define rms values of voltage and current with their phasor diagrams.
blocks.explanation:
rms current: the constant (DC) current that produces the same power in a resistor as the alternating current; Iᵣₘₛ = Iₒ/√2 = 0.707 Iₒ. rms voltage likewise: Vᵣₘₛ = Vₒ/√2 = 0.707 Vₒ.
Phasor diagram: each quantity is a vector rotating anticlockwise with angular frequency ω, its length equal to the peak (or rms = 0.707 × peak) value; for a resistor the V and I phasors lie along the same line (in phase).

blocks.prompt: 17.7 Resonance in LRC-circuits has various applications, give any four of them.
blocks.explanation:
1. Tuning radio and TV receivers to one station's frequency.
2. Band-pass filters in communication devices (pass a chosen frequency range, reject others).
3. Voltage amplification in series LRC circuits (V_L and V_C larger than the source voltage).
4. Induction cooktops and induction heating (parallel LRC circuit; also current magnification).

blocks.prompt: 17.1 What do you mean by rating of electrical appliances? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Rating is the set of values marked on an appliance by the manufacturer (power in watts, operating voltage, and often current and frequency) at which it works safely and efficiently.
Example: a heater rated "1000 W, 250 V" uses 1000 J of energy per second when connected to 250 V; it then draws I = P/V = 4 A (Example 17.3).
Using it at a higher voltage can overheat and damage it; at a lower voltage it gives less power. The rating helps to choose the correct fuse and wiring and to work out the energy used (kWh = kW × hours).

blocks.prompt: 17.2 The energy stored in an inductor is analogous to the kinetic energy of a moving mass? Justify.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. Energy in an inductor Uₘ = ½LI² has the same form as kinetic energy K.E. = ½mv²: inductance L plays the role of mass m and current I the role of velocity v.
Just as mass (inertia) opposes a change in velocity, inductance opposes a change in current (back emf ε = −L ΔI/Δt). Work is needed to build up the current, as to speed up a mass; the energy is stored in the magnetic field while the current flows and is given back when the current falls, as a moving body gives back its K.E. when it slows down.

rows: L opposes change in current (back emf)
Energy stored in the magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 17.3 What are safety measures to take when working with AC or DC?
blocks.explanation:
1. Switch off the supply (remove the fuse or open the breaker) before working on a circuit, and check with a tester that it is dead.
2. Use tools with insulated handles, rubber gloves and shoes, and stand on a dry insulating mat; never work with wet hands.
3. Earth all metal bodies of appliances and use fuses, circuit breakers and earth-leakage breakers of the correct rating.
4. Use wires and plugs of the proper current rating; avoid overloading sockets and replace damaged insulation.
5. Prefer low voltages where possible (e.g. a 12 V AC doorbell), since low voltage reduces the risk of shock.
6. In DC circuits discharge large capacitors before touching them and handle batteries carefully (short-circuits cause sparks and heat).
7. Keep one hand away from the circuit so that current cannot pass across the chest and heart. (mostly beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: 17.4 When the frequency is at “off resonance” in LCR-series circuit, the voltages across the inductor and capacitor can be significantly larger than the source voltage? Justify.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. V_L = IX_L and V_C = IX_C, but V_L leads the current by 90° and V_C lags by 90°, so they are 180° out of phase and subtract:
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
The source supplies only the difference V_L − V_C, while each of V_L and V_C on its own can be much larger. This happens whenever X_L and X_C are large compared with the impedance Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²), i.e. near resonance as well as at it.
Example: R = 24 Ω, X_L = 120 Ω, X_C = 150 Ω on 220 V (not at resonance): Z = √(24² + 30²) = 38.4 Ω, I = 220 V/38.4 Ω = 5.73 A, V_L = 5.73 A × 120 Ω = 687 V and V_C = 5.73 A × 150 Ω = 859 V, both much larger than 220 V.
Far from resonance (when one reactance is much larger than the other) this effect becomes small.

blocks.prompt: 17.5 How does self-induction manifest when a current is switched on or off in a circuit?
blocks.explanation:
Self-induction: a changing current in a coil induces an emf in the same coil, ε_L = −L ΔI/Δt, which opposes the change (Lenz's law).
Switch on: the current starts rising from zero; the induced back emf opposes the rise, so the current grows gradually to its steady value instead of instantly (a lamp in series with a large coil lights up late).
Switch off: the current falls to zero very quickly, so ΔI/Δt is very large and a large emf is induced in the direction of the original current, trying to keep it flowing; this can cause a spark across the switch contacts. The energy ½LI² stored in the magnetic field is released.

blocks.prompt: 17.6 Is it possible to achieve mutual inductance using a combination of four coils? If yes, justify your answer.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. Mutual induction needs only that the changing magnetic flux of one coil links another coil; it does not depend on how many coils there are.
With four coils (e.g. one primary and three secondaries wound on a common soft-iron core, as in a transformer with several windings), a changing current in the primary induces an emf in each of the other three: εₛ = −M ΔIₚ/Δt for each pair.
Every pair of coils has its own mutual inductance M, which depends on their numbers of turns, areas, distance, orientation and the core material (17.17). Using a common iron core makes all the coils share nearly the same flux, so the coupling is strong.

blocks.prompt: 17.7 The currents of the order of 0.1 A through human body is fatal what causes death; heating due to current or something else?
blocks.explanation:
Not mainly heating. The heating I²R produced by 0.1 A in the body is only a few watts, too little to kill quickly.
Death is caused by the current interfering with the body's electrical signals: the heart is driven by small electric pulses, and an external current of about 0.1 A through the chest upsets its rhythm (ventricular fibrillation), so the heart stops pumping blood. It can also paralyse the muscles used for breathing. AC at 50 Hz is especially dangerous because its frequency disturbs the heart's own pulses. (the term ventricular fibrillation is beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: 17.1 Explain the behaviour of a capacitor is an AC circuit. Derive the expression for capacitive reactance and discuss why current leads the voltage by 90° or π/2 rad.
blocks.explanation:
Behaviour of a capacitor in AC:
A capacitor does not pass DC because of the insulating medium between its plates. With an AC source the capacitor is charged first in one direction and then in the other as the voltage reverses, so electrons move to and fro in the connecting wires: an alternating current flows in the circuit. The capacitor stores energy in its electric field.
Derivation:
Applied voltage: V = Vₒ sin ωt   (17.18)
Charge at any instant: q = CV = CVₒ sin ωt
Current: I = Δq/Δt = CVₒ (Δ/Δt)(sin ωt)
As (Δ/Δt) sin ωt = ω cos ωt:
I = ωCVₒ cos ωt
As cos ωt = sin (ωt + π/2) and ωCVₒ = Iₒ:
I = Iₒ sin (ωt + π/2)   (17.19)
Capacitive reactance:
X_C = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707Vₒ/0.707Iₒ = Vₒ/Iₒ
As Iₒ = ωCVₒ:
X_C = Vₒ/ωCVₒ = 1/ωC = 1/2πfC   (unit: ohm)
X_C is large at low frequency (infinite for DC, f = 0) and small at high frequency, so a capacitor blocks DC and passes AC; at high frequency the current through it is large.
Why the current leads by 90°:
Comparing V = Vₒ sin ωt with I = Iₒ sin (ωt + π/2), the current reaches each value a quarter-cycle (T/4) before the voltage. Physically, the current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Δq/Δt = C ΔV/Δt. When V = 0 and rising, the voltage changes fastest, so charge flows onto the plates at the greatest rate: the current is maximum. When V reaches its peak, the capacitor is fully charged and the charge momentarily stops changing: the current is zero. So the current always peaks 90° (π/2 rad) before the voltage. In the phasor diagram the current vector is drawn 90° anticlockwise ahead of the voltage vector.
Power: average power in a pure capacitor is zero (P = VI cos 90° = 0); the energy stored in the electric field in one quarter-cycle is returned to the source in the next.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "behaviour of a capacitor is an AC circuit"; it means "in an AC circuit".

blocks.prompt: 17.2 Explain the behaviour of an inductor is an AC circuit. Derive the expression for inductive reactance and explain why current lags behind the voltage by 90° or π/2 rad.
blocks.explanation:
Behaviour of an inductor in AC:
An inductor (coil, choke) has a large self-inductance and negligible resistance. A changing current in it sets up a back emf that opposes the change, so it opposes AC; it stores energy in its magnetic field and returns it, so a pure inductor dissipates no average power. For DC (f = 0) it acts as a conductor.
Derivation:
Current: I = Iₒ sin ωt   (17.13)
Back emf: ε = L ΔI/Δt; to maintain the current the applied voltage must equal it:
V = L (Δ/Δt)(Iₒ sin ωt) = LIₒ (Δ/Δt) sin ωt   (17.14)
As (Δ/Δt) sin ωt = ω cos ωt:
V = ωLIₒ cos ωt
As ωLIₒ = Vₒ and cos ωt = sin (ωt + π/2):
V = Vₒ sin (ωt + π/2)   (17.15)
Inductive reactance:
X_L = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707Vₒ/0.707Iₒ = Vₒ/Iₒ
As Vₒ = ωLIₒ:
X_L = ωLIₒ/Iₒ = ωL = 2πfL   (17.17)   (unit: ohm)
X_L is directly proportional to the frequency and to L: for DC (f = 0) X_L = 0, and at high frequency X_L is large. So an inductor passes DC but opposes (blocks) high-frequency AC.
Why the current lags by 90°:
Comparing I = Iₒ sin ωt with V = Vₒ sin (ωt + π/2), the voltage reaches each value a quarter-cycle (T/4) before the current, i.e. the current lags by 90°. Physically, the voltage across the inductor equals L ΔI/Δt, the slope of the I-t curve. The slope is greatest when the current is zero (crossing the axis), so the voltage is then maximum; when the current is at its peak its slope is zero, so the voltage is zero. The back emf opposes every change of current, so the current builds up only after the voltage has been applied: it always reaches its peak 90° (π/2 rad) after the voltage. In the phasor diagram the current vector is 90° behind the voltage vector.
Power: average power is zero (P = VI cos 90° = 0); energy stored in the magnetic field in one quarter-cycle is returned in the next. Hence inductors (chokes) control AC without wasting energy.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "behaviour of an inductor is an AC circuit"; it means "in an AC circuit".

blocks.prompt: 17.3 Define RLC-parallel circuit. Also write its key properties.
blocks.explanation:
RLC-parallel circuit: a circuit in which a resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C are connected in parallel to each other across an AC source. The voltage is the same across all three, and the source current divides among the branches.
Key properties:
1. Resonance and impedance: the circuit resonates when X_L = X_C; the impedance is then maximum (Z = R) and the circuit behaves as purely resistive. Its impedance is
Z = 1/√((1/R)² + (1/X_L − 1/X_C)²)
2. Voltage and current: the voltage is the same across all components, so it is taken as the reference phasor. At resonance the source current is minimum, while the branch currents I_L and I_C may each be much larger than it (current magnification).
3. Admittance: admittance Y = 1/Z is used to analyse parallel circuits; the total admittance is the sum of the admittances of the individual components.
4. Frequency and bandwidth: the impedance, admittance and currents all depend on frequency; the bandwidth is the range of frequencies over which the circuit works effectively. Resonance frequency:
fᵣ = 1/(2π√LC)
5. Quality factor Q: a measure of the sharpness of the resonance peak (energy stored compared with energy dissipated). For a parallel circuit Q = R√(C/L), so a larger R gives a sharper peak.
6. Power factor: depends on frequency and on the relative sizes of X_L and X_C; at resonance it is unity (1).
Uses: tuning circuits, signal processing, power systems and induction cooktops (the resonant circuit drives a high-frequency current in the coil that heats the metal pan).

blocks.prompt: 17.4 Find expression for impedance in case of RC and RL-series circuits.
blocks.explanation:
(a) RC-series circuit
R and C are in series with an AC source, so the same current Iᵣₘₛ flows through both; take the current as reference.
Voltage across R: V_R = IᵣₘₛR, in phase with the current (drawn along the current line).
Voltage across C: V_C = IᵣₘₛX_C = Iᵣₘₛ/ωC, lagging the current by 90° (drawn at right angles).
The applied voltage is the vector sum:
Vᵣₘₛ = √(V_R² + V_C²) = √((IᵣₘₛR)² + (Iᵣₘₛ/ωC)²) = Iᵣₘₛ √(R² + (1/ωC)²)
Impedance Z = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = √(R² + (1/ωC)²) = √(R² + X_C²)   (17.21)
Phase angle: θ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R) = tan⁻¹(1/ωCR); the current leads the applied voltage by θ.
(b) RL-series circuit
The same current Iᵣₘₛ flows through R and L.
Voltage across R: V_R = IᵣₘₛR, in phase with the current (line OA).
Voltage across L: V_L = IᵣₘₛX_L = IᵣₘₛωL, leading the current by 90° (line OB).
The applied voltage is the vector sum (line OP):
Vᵣₘₛ = √(V_R² + V_L²) = √((IᵣₘₛR)² + (IᵣₘₛωL)²) = Iᵣₘₛ √(R² + (ωL)²)
Impedance Z = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = √(R² + (ωL)²) = √(R² + X_L²)   (17.23)
Phase angle: θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R); the applied voltage leads the current by θ.
In both cases the impedance (unit ohm) is found by vector addition of resistance and reactance in the impedance diagram, and the power is P = I²R = VI cos θ.

blocks.prompt: 17.5 Define full-wave rectification? Draw circuit, input and output signal phasor diagrams to explain how full-wave rectification is achieved by use of full wave bridge rectifier.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: rectification during which both halves of the alternating input voltage are converted into a unidirectional current through a load resistance is called full-wave rectification.
Circuit (bridge rectifier), to be drawn:
Four diodes D₁, D₂, D₃, D₄ are connected in a closed loop (a diamond-shaped "bridge"). The AC input (the secondary winding of a transformer) is connected to two opposite corners A and B of the bridge; the load resistance R is connected between the other two corners. The diodes form two "series pairs": D₁ and D₂, and D₃ and D₄, with only one pair conducting in each half-cycle.
Working:
Positive half-cycle (0 → T/2): terminal A is positive with respect to B. D₁ and D₂ are forward biased and conduct in series; D₃ and D₄ are reverse biased. Current flows through R in one direction.
Negative half-cycle (T/2 → T): A is negative and B positive. D₃ and D₄ conduct in series; D₁ and D₂ are reverse biased (OFF). The current through R flows in the same direction as before.
Signals (graphs) to be drawn:
Input: a sine wave of period T, positive from 0 to T/2 and negative from T/2 to T.
Output across R: positive humps in every half-cycle; the negative half-cycles appear inverted as positive humps, so there are two pulses per input cycle (the ripple frequency is 2f). The current is unidirectional but pulsating.
Smoothing: a capacitor connected in parallel with the load charges when the rectified voltage rises and discharges when it falls, so the output becomes a nearly steady DC with a small ripple, V_ripple = I_DC/(2fC).
Use: mobile phone chargers and DC power supplies use a full-wave bridge rectifier.

blocks.prompt: 17.6 State and explain in detail RLC-series circuit?
blocks.explanation:
RLC-series circuit: a resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C connected in series with an AC source (of variable frequency). The same current I flows through all three.
Phasor (vector) diagram, with the current as reference:
V_R = IR, in phase with I
V_L = IX_L = IωL, leading I by 90°
V_C = IX_C = I/ωC, lagging I by 90°
V_L and V_C are opposite (180° apart), so the net reactive voltage is V_L − V_C. The applied voltage:
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
Impedance:
Z = V/I = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)   (17.24)
Z = √(R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²)   (17.25)
Phase angle: tan θ = (X_L − X_C)/R = (V_L − V_C)/V_R
Behaviour with frequency:
High frequency: X_L = ωL ≫ X_C, the inductance dominates and the circuit behaves as an RL-series circuit (voltage leads current).
Low frequency: X_C = 1/ωC ≫ X_L, the capacitance dominates and it behaves as an RC-series circuit (current leads voltage).
Resonance: at one frequency X_L = X_C; they cancel and the circuit behaves as purely resistive.
ωᵣL = 1/ωᵣC, ωᵣ² = 1/LC, ωᵣ = 1/√LC
fᵣ = 1/(2π√LC)   (17.26)
Key properties:
1. At resonance the impedance is minimum, Z = R.
2. The current is maximum at resonance (minimum impedance).
3. The phase angle is zero at resonance: V and I in phase, power factor 1.
4. Damping: R damps the oscillations; a larger R gives more damping (like the shock absorber of a car's wheel on its spring).
5. Tuning and filtering: used for tuning radio receivers and as band-pass filters.
6. Voltage amplification: at resonance V_L and V_C can be much larger than the applied voltage.
7. Power: P = VI cos θ (true power), maximum when θ = 0; the apparent power is VI (volt-ampere).
Example 17.7: V_L = 20 V, V_C = 11 V, V_R = 12 V give tan θ = 9/12 = 0.75, θ = 36.8°, and V = √(12² + 9²) = 15 V.

blocks.prompt:
17.1 AC circuit configure by a resistance of 20 Ω, capacitor of capacitance 40 μF is connected to an AC supply of 110 V having frequency 50 Hz. Calculate: (a) capacitive reactance. (b) current in the circuits (c) suggest phase between the voltage and current in a capacitive circuit.
(Ans: (a) 79.58 Ω (b) 1.34A (c) Current leads voltage by 90° or π / 2 rad.)
blocks.explanation:
Given: R = 20 Ω, C = 40 μF = 40 × 10⁻⁶ F, Vᵣₘₛ = 110 V, f = 50 Hz (R and C in series)
Required: (a) X_C (b) Iᵣₘₛ (c) phase
(a) X_C = 1/2πfC
X_C = 1/(2 × 3.1416 × 50 Hz × 40 × 10⁻⁶ F)
X_C = 1/(0.012566 Ω⁻¹)
X_C = 79.58 Ω
(b) Impedance of the RC-series circuit:
Z = √(R² + X_C²) = √((20 Ω)² + (79.58 Ω)²)
Z = √(400 + 6332.7) Ω = √6732.7 Ω = 82.05 Ω
Iᵣₘₛ = Vᵣₘₛ/Z = 110 V/82.05 Ω
Iᵣₘₛ = 1.34 A
(c) In a capacitive circuit the current leads the voltage by 90° (π/2 rad): across the capacitor itself, I = Iₒ sin (ωt + π/2).
For this whole RC circuit, the current leads the supply voltage by θ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R) = tan⁻¹(79.58/20) = tan⁻¹(3.98) = 75.9°.
Answer: (a) 79.58 Ω (b) 1.34 A (c) current leads voltage by 90° (π/2 rad) for the capacitor; 75.9° for the RC circuit as a whole (agrees with the book).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "configure" and "current in the circuits"; read "configured" and "current in the circuit". The printed answer (c), 90°, is the phase for the capacitor; for the RC circuit as a whole the current leads the supply voltage by 75.9°.

blocks.prompt:
17.2 An alternating current I is represented by the equation; I = 420 sin (100 πt).Find (a) the rms current (b) the frequency
(Ans: (a) 296.94 A (b) = 50 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: I = 420 sin (100πt); compare with I = Iₒ sin ωt
Iₒ = 420 A, ω = 100π rad s⁻¹
Required: (a) Iᵣₘₛ (b) f
(a) Iᵣₘₛ = Iₒ/√2 = 0.707 Iₒ
Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707 × 420 A
Iᵣₘₛ = 296.94 A ≈ 297 A
(b) ω = 2πf, so f = ω/2π
f = 100π/2π
f = 50 Hz
Answer: (a) 296.94 A (b) 50 Hz (agrees with the book; with 1/√2 exactly, Iᵣₘₛ = 296.98 A).

blocks.prompt:
17.3 A 50 Hz AC of peak value 1 A flows through primary coil of a transformer. If the mutual inductance between the primary and secondary be 1.5 H, then find the mean value of induced voltage.
(Ans: 3000 V)
blocks.explanation:
Given: f = 50 Hz, Iₒ = 1 A, M = 1.5 H
Required: mean induced emf ε
Time period: T = 1/f = 1/50 Hz = 0.02 s
The current rises from 0 to its peak 1 A in a quarter-cycle:
Δt = T/4 = 0.02 s/4 = 0.005 s
ΔIₚ = 1 A − 0 = 1 A
Mean rate of change: ΔIₚ/Δt = 1 A/0.005 s = 200 A s⁻¹
Mean induced emf (Eq. 17.41, magnitude):
ε = M ΔIₚ/Δt
ε = 1.5 H × 200 A s⁻¹
ε = 300 V
Check: peak emf = MωIₒ = 1.5 H × 314.2 rad s⁻¹ × 1 A = 471 V; half-cycle mean = 0.637 × 471 V = 300 V.
Answer: 300 V (the book prints 3000 V; see the box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's answer is printed 3000 V. With M = 1.5 H, ΔI = 1 A in a quarter-cycle Δt = T/4 = 0.005 s, the mean emf is ε = MΔI/Δt = 1.5 × 200 = 300 V (the same as 0.637 × the peak emf MωIₒ = 471 V). 3000 V would need a frequency of 500 Hz.

blocks.prompt:
17.4 A 220 V AC source of frequency 2 kHz is connected across a capacitor of 10 μF. Find out: (a) the reactance X_L of capacitor (b) the current in the circuit.
(Ans: (a) 7.96 Ω (b) 27.63 A)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 220 V, f = 2 kHz = 2000 Hz, C = 10 μF = 10 × 10⁻⁶ F
Required: (a) capacitive reactance X_C (b) I
(a) X_C = 1/2πfC
X_C = 1/(2 × 3.1416 × 2000 Hz × 10 × 10⁻⁶ F)
X_C = 1/(0.12566 Ω⁻¹)
X_C = 7.96 Ω
(b) I = V/X_C
I = 220 V/7.96 Ω
I = 27.64 A ≈ 27.6 A
Answer: (a) 7.96 Ω (b) 27.6 A (agrees with the book; it prints 27.63 A, a rounding difference).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "the reactance X_L of capacitor". A capacitor's reactance is the capacitive reactance X_C (X_L is the inductive reactance).

blocks.prompt:
17.5 In a coil of inductance 150 mH, a current changes steadily from 50 mA to 30 mA in 164 ms, find: (a) the magnitude (b) direction of induced emf.
(Ans: (a) 18.29 mV (b) same direction as the original current.)
blocks.explanation:
Given: L = 150 mH = 0.150 H, I₁ = 50 mA, I₂ = 30 mA, Δt = 164 ms = 0.164 s
Required: (a) |ε| (b) direction
ΔI = I₂ − I₁ = 30 mA − 50 mA = −20 mA = −0.020 A
(a) ε = −L ΔI/Δt   (17.31)
ε = −0.150 H × (−0.020 A/0.164 s)
ε = 0.150 H × 0.1220 A s⁻¹
ε = 0.01829 V = 18.29 mV
(b) The current is decreasing, so by Lenz's law the induced emf opposes the decrease: it tries to keep the current flowing, i.e. it acts in the same direction as the original current (ε is positive while ΔI is negative).
Answer: (a) 18.29 mV (b) in the same direction as the original current (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
17.6 A choke coil is needed to operate a lamp at 160 Vᵣₘₛ and 50 Hz. The lamp has an resistance of 5 Ω when running at 10 Aᵣₘₛ. Calculate the inductance of the choke coil.
(Ans: 48.4 mH)
blocks.explanation:
Given: Vᵣₘₛ = 160 V, f = 50 Hz, R = 5 Ω (lamp), Iᵣₘₛ = 10 A; the choke (pure inductor) is in series with the lamp
Required: L
Voltage across the lamp: V_R = IR = 10 A × 5 Ω = 50 V
In an RL-series circuit: V² = V_R² + V_L²
V_L = √(V² − V_R²) = √((160 V)² − (50 V)²)
V_L = √(25600 − 2500) V = √23100 V = 152 V
X_L = V_L/I = 152 V/10 A = 15.2 Ω
X_L = 2πfL, so L = X_L/2πf
L = 15.2 Ω/(2 × 3.1416 × 50 Hz)
L = 15.2 Ω/314.16 s⁻¹
L = 0.0484 H = 48.4 mH
Answer: L = 48.4 mH (agrees with the book).
